decks.title: Evolution — Part 1: Traits, natural selection and the origin of species
goals: Distinguish acquired traits from inherited traits with examples
Explain how natural selection changes a population over generations
Explain genetic drift and how it differs from natural selection
Explain how geographical isolation, genetic drift and natural selection lead to new species

slides.heading: Evolution
slides.body_md: Part 1 — which traits can be passed on, and how populations change until new species arise. (This chapter is assessed through school-based activities and projects, not the board theory paper.)

nodes.label: Some variants survive and reproduce more

visual.alt: Flow from variation to inheritance to selection to change in a population

slides.narration: Namaste! Why are there tigers and sparrows, mango trees and mushrooms, and not just one kind of living thing? Life on Earth has been changing for billions of years. This slow change in the inherited features of populations, over many generations, is called evolution. In this lesson we see which features can be passed on, and how new species arise.

slides.heading: What evolution is, and what it is not
slides.body_md: **Evolution** is the change in the **inherited characteristics of a population** over **many generations**. Individuals grow and change during their lives, but only **populations** evolve.

rows: A child grows taller every year
A cricketer’s arms become strong with practice
Over 40 years, most mosquitoes in a town survive an insecticide
Inherited change in a population over generations

visual.alt: Table of three situations, only one of which, an inherited change in a mosquito population over generations, is evolution

slides.narration: Be careful with the word evolution. When you grow taller, you are developing, not evolving. Evolution happens to populations, not to individuals, and it needs many generations. If, over forty years, most mosquitoes in a town become able to survive an insecticide, the population has evolved, because the change is inherited.

slides.heading: Acquired and inherited traits
slides.body_md: An **acquired trait** develops during an individual’s **lifetime**, through use, training, injury or surroundings. An **inherited trait** comes from the **DNA** received from the parents. Only inherited traits are passed on.

rows: During an individual’s life, through use, training, injury or surroundings
From the DNA received from the parents
Changes the DNA of germ cells?
Strong muscles from exercise, a scar, a language learnt, a trimmed tail
Blood group, natural eye colour, flower colour in peas

visual.alt: Table comparing acquired and inherited traits: how they arise, whether they change germ-cell DNA, whether they are passed on, and examples

slides.narration: Think of a weightlifter. Years of training build big muscles. That is an acquired trait: it was earned, not inherited, and the weightlifter’s children will not be born with those muscles. But blood group or natural eye colour come from the DNA you received from your parents. Those inherited traits can pass on to your children.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sorting traits
slides.body_md: Sort these traits of a girl named Asha: (1) blood group B, (2) fluency in Tamil and English, (3) a scar on her knee from a fall, (4) naturally curly hair, (5) strong lungs from swimming practice.
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: did it come from DNA received at fertilisation, or did it develop during life?
Step 2 — Blood group and naturally curly hair come from DNA: **inherited**.
Step 3 — Languages, the scar and swimming-trained lungs developed during life: **acquired**.
Conclusion — only blood group and curly hair can be passed to Asha’s children through her genes.

headers: Can pass to children through genes?

visual.alt: Worked table sorting five of Asha’s traits into inherited and acquired, and whether each can be passed on

slides.narration: Use one simple test: did this trait come from the DNA Asha got from her parents, or did it develop because of something that happened during her life? Languages are learnt, scars come from accidents, and swimming builds the lungs. None of these change the DNA in her egg cells. Children may learn Tamil from Asha, but not through genes.

slides.heading: Why acquired traits are not inherited
slides.body_md: Offspring develop from **germ cells** (egg and sperm). Changes in **body tissues**, such as muscles or skin, do **not** change the **DNA in germ cells**, so they cannot be passed on.

nodes.label: Change in body tissue (muscle, skin, tail)
Offspring do not show the change

visual.alt: Flow: a change in body tissue leaves germ-cell DNA unchanged, so offspring, which develop from germ cells, do not show the change

slides.narration: In the eighteen eighties, a scientist cut off the tails of mice, generation after generation. Every new litter was still born with full tails. The cutting changed the bodies of the parents, but not the DNA in their sperm and eggs. Only changes in the DNA of germ cells can be inherited. That is the key to the whole of evolution.

slides.heading: Quick check: can a skill be inherited?
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement about a trained rat is true or false.
slides.narration: Quick check. Was the skill written into the DNA of the rat’s germ cells, or learnt during its life?

slides.heading: Natural selection in action
slides.body_md: Imagine grasshoppers on grassland that has turned **dry and brown**. Some are **green** and some **brown**, because of differences in their DNA. Birds spot the green ones easily. More brown grasshoppers **survive and breed**, so over generations **brown becomes common**.

visual.alt: Two panels of grasshoppers on dry brown grass: half green and half brown in the first generation, and mostly brown several generations later
visual.caption: An illustrative population; birds are the selecting agent.

slides.narration: No grasshopper chose its colour, and none changed colour to hide. The variation was already there. Birds simply ate more of the easy-to-see green ones. The brown survivors laid more eggs, and their young inherited brown colour. Generation after generation, the population shifted. This is natural selection: nature, here the birds, selects which variations survive.

slides.heading: Natural selection step by step
slides.body_md: Natural selection explains how populations become **better suited** to their surroundings. It works only on **inherited variations**.

rows: Individuals differ, partly because of differences in their DNA
More young are born than can survive
Some variations help individuals survive and reproduce better in that environment
Survivors pass these variations to their offspring
Over generations, the useful variations become common in the population

visual.alt: Table of the five steps of natural selection: variation, too many offspring, struggle, inheritance and change over generations

slides.narration: Here is the logic in five steps. Individuals vary. More young are born than can survive. Those whose variations suit the surroundings survive and breed more. They pass on those variations. Over many generations, the useful variations spread. Notice that nothing in these steps needs an animal to want or try to change.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: tracking a population
slides.body_md: A population has 100 green and 100 brown grasshoppers on brown grass. Birds eat half of the green ones and one tenth of the brown ones. What percentage of the survivors are brown?
bullets: Step 1 — Green survivors $= 100 - 50 = 50$; brown survivors $= 100 - 10 = 90$.
Step 2 — Total survivors $= 50 + 90 = 140$.
Step 3 — Brown share $= \dfrac{90}{140} \times 100 \approx 64\%$.
Conclusion — brown rose from 50% to about 64% in one generation; if survivors breed equally, the next generation starts at about 64% brown.

visual.alt: Worked table: of 100 green and 100 brown grasshoppers, 50 green and 90 brown survive, so the brown share rises from 50 to about 64 per cent

slides.narration: Numbers make selection visible. Before the birds came, the population was half and half. After one season, ninety brown and fifty green survive, so about sixty-four per cent are brown. If those survivors breed equally, the next generation is mostly brown too. Repeat this for a few more seasons, and green becomes rare.

slides.heading: Genetic drift: change by chance
slides.body_md: **Genetic drift** is a **random change** in how common a variation is, caused by **chance** events such as which individuals happen to survive or breed. It gives **no survival advantage** and is strongest in **small populations**.

rows: Some variants survive and reproduce better
Pure chance (accidents, which individuals happen to breed)
Yes: favours variations that suit the environment
No: the change gives no survival advantage

visual.alt: Table comparing natural selection and genetic drift by cause of change, whether the change is adaptive, and where it is strongest

slides.narration: Picture a tiny population of twenty beetles on a rock. A boulder rolls down and crushes twelve of them by sheer bad luck. If most of the eight survivors happen to be red, the next generation will be mostly red, not because red is better, but by chance. In a large population, such accidents average out. In a small one, chance can change the population a lot.

slides.heading: What is a species?
slides.body_md: A **species** is a group of organisms whose members can **interbreed** and produce **fertile offspring**. **Speciation** is the formation of a new species from an existing one. It needs the flow of genes between parts of a population to **stop**.

rows: Members can interbreed and have fertile young
Mixing of genes when members of different groups interbreed
Two groups can no longer interbreed successfully

visual.alt: Table of four terms: species, gene flow, speciation and reproductive isolation, with their meanings

slides.narration: Dogs of every breed, from tiny to huge, belong to one species, because they can interbreed and have fertile puppies. Horses and donkeys can produce mules, but mules are usually sterile, so horses and donkeys are separate species. As long as genes keep flowing between groups, they stay one species.

slides.heading: How a new species arises
slides.body_md: When a barrier such as a river or mountain **splits** a population, **gene flow stops**. Each part then changes separately through **genetic drift** and **natural selection**. After many generations, they may become so different that they **cannot interbreed**: two species.

visual.alt: Four stages of speciation: one population, split by a river, changing separately on each side, until the two parts can no longer interbreed

slides.narration: Follow the four stages. One population of, say, snails lives on a plain. A river changes course and splits it. Snails cannot cross water, so the two parts stop mixing genes. On each bank, chance and different surroundings change the populations in different ways. Given enough time, even if the river dries up, they can no longer interbreed.

slides.heading: Factors that lead to speciation
slides.body_md: Several factors work together to produce new species.

rows: Stops gene flow between the two parts of a population
Chance changes in each isolated part, especially if it is small
Different surroundings favour different variations in each part
Germ cells of the two groups can no longer combine successfully

visual.alt: Table of four factors in speciation with their effects: isolation stops gene flow, drift and selection make the parts differ, and DNA changes prevent interbreeding

slides.narration: Isolation is usually the first step, because it stops genes from mixing. Then drift and selection push the two groups apart. Finally, changes build up in the DNA, sometimes even in the number of chromosomes, so that the germ cells of the two groups can no longer combine to make healthy, fertile young. At that point, speciation is complete.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: one species or two?
slides.body_md: Two groups of tree frogs live in neighbouring forests. Over thousands of years their mating calls became different, and females now respond only to their own group’s call. When kept together, they never mate. Are they still one species?
bullets: Step 1 — The test for a species is whether members can interbreed and produce fertile young.
Step 2 — Here the two groups never mate, even when they meet, so no genes flow between them.
Step 3 — Different calls are a form of **reproductive isolation**.
Conclusion — they now behave as **two separate species**; each will go on changing in its own way.

rows: Behaviour has changed in each group
Females respond only to own call

visual.alt: Worked table linking the frogs’ different calls and lack of mating to reproductive isolation

slides.narration: Here is a subtle point. A river or mountain is not the only barrier. Once the frogs’ calls differ, a female simply ignores males of the other group. No genes cross over, even though the two groups can meet. A barrier in behaviour works just like a barrier of water. So the frogs now behave as two species.

slides.heading: Quick check: what stops gene flow?
slides.body_md: Which event is most likely to stop gene flow between two parts of a population of land snails?
slides.narration: Your turn. Think about what physically stops snails from meeting and mating.

slides.heading: Common misunderstandings
slides.body_md: Evolution is often described wrongly. Here are the scientific ideas.

rows: Animals change because they need to
Variations arise by chance; selection keeps the useful ones
Only changes in germ-cell DNA are inherited
Evolution produces diversity, suited to surroundings

visual.alt: Table of four common misunderstandings about evolution with the correct scientific ideas

slides.narration: Watch out for these traps. Grasshoppers did not turn brown because they needed to hide. Giraffes did not stretch their necks and pass the stretch on. Need and effort do not change DNA. Variations arise by chance, and the surroundings decide which ones last. And evolution is not a ladder towards perfection; bacteria are as evolved as we are.

slides.heading: Quick check: drift and population size
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about genetic drift.
slides.narration: Quick check. Are both statements true? Does the second explain the first?

slides.heading: Summary: traits, selection and speciation
bullets: Evolution: change in the inherited traits of a population over many generations.
Acquired traits develop during life and are not inherited; inherited traits come from DNA.
Only changes in germ-cell DNA pass to offspring.
Natural selection: variants that survive and reproduce better become common.
Genetic drift: chance changes, strongest in small populations.
Speciation: isolation stops gene flow; drift, selection and DNA changes make groups unable to interbreed.

rows: Not in germ-cell DNA, not inherited

visual.alt: Summary table of acquired traits, natural selection, genetic drift and speciation

slides.narration: Let us recap. Only inherited traits, written in the DNA of germ cells, can be passed on. Natural selection spreads useful variations, while genetic drift changes small populations by chance. When gene flow stops, the separated groups change in different ways, and given enough time, they become new species that can no longer interbreed.

slides.heading: Exam tips: traits and speciation
bullets: When classifying a trait, ask: **does it come from DNA, or did it develop during life?**
Explain why acquired traits are not inherited using **germ cells**: body changes do not alter germ-cell DNA.
In natural selection answers, say the variation **already existed**; avoid "they needed to change".
Define a species by **interbreeding and fertile offspring**.
For speciation, mention **isolation → no gene flow → drift and selection → reproductive isolation**.

rows: Brown variants already existed and survived better
Acquired traits are not inherited because they are new
They do not change the DNA of germ cells
A river stops gene flow, so the parts change separately

visual.alt: Table contrasting weak and strong exam answers about evolution

slides.narration: Examiners look for precise language. Never write that an animal changed because it needed to. Write that a variation already existed and was selected. Link inheritance to the DNA of germ cells. And for speciation, tell the whole chain: isolation stops gene flow, then drift and selection make the groups different, until they can no longer interbreed.

decks.title: Evolution — Part 2: Tracing relationships, fossils and human evolution
goals: Explain how shared characteristics show evolutionary relationships
Distinguish homologous and analogous organs with examples
Explain what fossils are and how their age is found
Explain how complex organs evolve in stages, and outline the common origin of humans

slides.heading: Tracing evolution
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how body structures, fossils and DNA reveal family relationships among living things, and where humans fit in.

visual.alt: Flow from shared characteristics to shared ancestors to classification and a family tree of life

slides.narration: Detectives solve cases with clues. Biologists tracing evolution use three kinds of clues: the structure of living bodies, the remains of ancient life preserved in rocks, and the DNA inside cells. In this lesson we read these clues to build a family tree of life, and to place ourselves on it correctly.

slides.heading: Classification follows evolution
slides.body_md: The **more characteristics** two kinds of organism share, the **more recently** they shared a **common ancestor**, and the more closely related they are. So classifying organisms by shared features also traces their **evolution**.

rows: Backbone, four limbs, hair, milk for young

visual.alt: Table comparing humans with a mouse, a frog and a fish by shared features, showing that more shared features mean a closer relationship

slides.narration: Compare yourself with a mouse, a frog and a fish. All four have a backbone. You, the mouse and the frog also have four limbs. But only you and the mouse have hair and feed your young with milk. The more features you share, the more recently your ancestors were the same. That is why classification and evolution tell the same story.

slides.heading: A family tree of vertebrates
slides.body_md: A **family tree** (phylogenetic tree) shows relationships as **branches**. Each branch point stands for a **common ancestor**. Features such as a backbone, four limbs, and hair and milk appear at the branch where they **first arose** and are shared by everything above that branch.

slides.heading: Homologous organs
slides.body_md: **Homologous organs** have the **same basic structure** and **origin** but may do **different jobs**. The forelimbs of a human, a cat, a whale and a bird all have one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones and finger bones, because they were **inherited from a common ancestor**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: homologous or analogous?
slides.body_md: Classify each pair: (1) flipper of a dolphin and arm of a human; (2) wing of a butterfly and wing of a sparrow; (3) potato (a stem) and sweet potato (a root), both storing food; (4) thorn of bougainvillea and tendril of a cucumber plant (both modified stems).
bullets: Step 1 — Ask: same basic structure and origin? If yes, **homologous**, whatever the job.
Step 2 — If the job is similar but the structure and origin differ, **analogous**.
Step 3 — (1) same forelimb bones: homologous. (2) different structures, both for flight: analogous.
Step 4 — (3) stem and root, both storing food: analogous. (4) both stems, different jobs: homologous.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four pairs of organs as homologous or analogous by origin and job

slides.narration: Always judge by origin, not by job or looks. A dolphin’s flipper looks nothing like your arm, yet it hides the same bones, so it is homologous. A potato and a sweet potato both store food, but one is a swollen stem and the other a swollen root, so they are analogous. The job can mislead you; the origin decides.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the homologous pair
slides.body_md: Which pair of organs is homologous?
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for the same basic structure, even if the job is different.

slides.heading: Fossils: life’s past in stone
slides.body_md: **Fossils** are the **preserved remains or traces** of organisms that lived long ago: bones, teeth, shells, impressions of leaves, footprints, even insects trapped in amber. Most form when remains are **buried in sediment** before they decay, and the sediment slowly turns to rock.

rows: Leaf prints in rock, feather imprints
Insects in amber, mammoths in frozen ground

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of fossil with examples: petrified hard parts, impressions, traces and whole bodies

slides.narration: When an animal dies, its body usually rots away. But if it is buried quickly, say in mud at the bottom of a lake, the hard parts may be replaced by minerals and turn to stone. Millions of years later, erosion or digging brings them to light. In India, fossil dinosaur eggs have been found in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.

slides.heading: Reading the rock layers
slides.body_md: Sedimentary rock forms in **layers**, one on top of another. In **undisturbed** rock, **deeper layers are older**, so fossils found deeper are generally older than those near the surface.

slides.narration: Think of a pile of newspapers that grows every day. The paper at the bottom is the oldest. Rock layers build up in the same way. So a trilobite fossil found deep below an ammonite tells us the trilobite lived earlier. This gives relative age, older or younger, but not yet a number of years.

slides.heading: Dating fossils
slides.body_md: There are two main ways of dating fossils.

rows: In undisturbed layers, deeper rock was laid down earlier
Compares the amounts of different isotopes of an element (for example carbon) in the fossil

visual.alt: Table of two ways of dating fossils: relative dating by depth and radioactive dating by isotope ratios

slides.narration: Depth tells us which fossil is older. For an actual age, scientists use radioactive dating. Some isotopes, such as carbon fourteen, slowly change into other atoms at a steady rate. By comparing the amounts of different isotopes in a fossil, scientists work out roughly how long ago the organism died. Carbon dating works only for remains up to some tens of thousands of years old.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dating with half-lives
slides.body_md: Half of the carbon-14 in dead material decays in about **5730 years** (its half-life). A piece of fossil wood has **one-eighth** of the carbon-14 that living wood has. Roughly how old is it?
bullets: Step 1 — After one half-life, $\dfrac{1}{2}$ remains; after two, $\dfrac{1}{4}$; after three, $\dfrac{1}{8}$.
Step 2 — So three half-lives have passed.
Step 3 — Age $\approx 3 \times 5730 = 17190$ years.
Answer — the wood is about **17 000 years** old.

visual.alt: Worked table: after one, two and three half-lives of 5730 years, a half, a quarter and an eighth of the carbon-14 remain

slides.narration: Halving is the key idea. Each half-life cuts what is left in half: a half, then a quarter, then an eighth. One-eighth means three halvings, so three times five thousand seven hundred and thirty years, about seventeen thousand years. Real dating is more careful, but this simple halving shows how the method works.

slides.heading: Archaeopteryx and the story of feathers
slides.body_md: Fossils of **Archaeopteryx** show **feathers** like a bird, but also **teeth**, **clawed fingers** on the wings and a **long bony tail** like a reptile. Fossils like this link **reptiles (dinosaurs) and birds**. Feathers were also found in some dinosaurs that could not fly; they probably first helped keep the body **warm**, and only later were used for **flight**.

visual.alt: Table of Archaeopteryx features, showing feathers like birds and teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail like reptiles

slides.narration: Archaeopteryx is a famous in-between fossil. It had feathered wings, yet its jaws had teeth and its wings had claws. Birds, it turns out, are a branch of the dinosaur family. And feathers did not appear for flying. Many dinosaurs had feathers, probably for warmth or display. Much later, feathers were put to a new use: flight.

slides.heading: Quick check: which fossil is older?
slides.body_md: Fossils are found at two depths in undisturbed rock. Which is older?
slides.narration: Your turn. Remember the pile of newspapers: which ones went down first?

slides.heading: Complex organs evolve in stages
slides.body_md: A complex organ such as the **eye** did not appear in one step. **Each stage was useful**: a light-sensitive patch, then a cup that shows the direction of light, then a lens that forms images. Eyes have evolved **separately** in many groups, such as octopuses, insects and vertebrates.

visual.alt: Flow of eye evolution in stages: a light-sensitive patch, a cup-shaped eye, a narrow opening and finally a lens eye

slides.narration: People sometimes ask: what use is half an eye? Quite a lot! A flatworm called planaria has simple eyespots that only tell light from dark, and that already helps it escape bright, exposed places. A cup shape tells the direction of light. A lens forms images. Every small improvement helped its owners survive, so selection built the eye step by step.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: wild cabbage to five vegetables
slides.body_md: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and kale all came from **wild cabbage** through **artificial selection**. Explain how farmers could produce kohlrabi.
bullets: Step 1 — Wild cabbage plants vary; some happen to have slightly thicker stems.
Step 2 — Farmers saved seeds only from plants with the thickest stems.
Step 3 — Repeating this for many generations made the stem more and more swollen.
Conclusion — the result is **kohlrabi**. Choosing different parts (leaves, buds, flowers) gave the other vegetables.

nodes.label: Cabbage: short stem, tightly packed leaves
Cauliflower: dense head of undeveloped flowers

visual.alt: Flow showing wild cabbage giving rise, through selection by farmers, to cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and kale
visual.caption: All five are still one species; farmers selected different parts of the plant.

slides.narration: This is selection with humans in charge. Farmers did not create new features; they picked plants that already varied a little and bred from them, generation after generation. Select for big leaves and you get kale. Select for a short stem with tightly packed leaves, and you get cabbage. Select for flower buds, and you get broccoli. It shows how much selection can change a species.

slides.heading: DNA as evidence: molecular phylogeny
slides.body_md: Today, scientists compare **DNA** directly. Changes build up in DNA over time, so **closely related** organisms have **more similar DNA**, and distant ones less similar. This **molecular phylogeny** confirms the family trees built from body structures and fossils.

rows: Very distant, yet some genes are still shared

visual.alt: Table showing that human DNA is most similar to chimpanzee DNA, less to mouse DNA and much less to banana DNA

slides.narration: DNA is like a family record written inside every cell. Two species that split recently have had little time to build up differences, so their DNA is very similar. Human and chimpanzee DNA are close to ninety-nine per cent alike. Even a banana plant shares some genes with us, because all life on Earth shares very ancient ancestors.

slides.heading: Humans and chimpanzees: cousins, not ancestors
slides.body_md: **Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees.** Humans and chimpanzees evolved from a **common ancestor** that lived **several million years ago**. Since then, each line has evolved separately; today’s chimpanzees are our **cousins**, not our ancestors.

slides.narration: This is the most common mistake about human evolution. Chimpanzees living today are not our grandparents; they are our cousins. Millions of years ago, one ancestral population split. One branch led to chimpanzees, the other to humans. Both have kept evolving ever since. In the same way, you and your cousin share grandparents, but neither of you descends from the other.

slides.heading: The origin of modern humans
slides.body_md: Fossil and DNA evidence shows that modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, arose in **Africa** a few hundred thousand years ago. Groups later **spread out of Africa** and across the world. All humans living today belong to **one species**: differences in skin colour, height or hair are **small variations**, not separate kinds of people.

nodes.label: Some groups leave Africa (tens of thousands of years ago)
Spread to Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas

visual.alt: Flow of human origins: Homo sapiens arises in Africa, groups leave Africa, spread across the continents, and remain one species

slides.narration: Every person on Earth, from Kashmir to Kanyakumari and from Peru to Japan, belongs to one species, Homo sapiens. Our species arose in Africa. Over tens of thousands of years, groups spread across Asia, Europe and Australia, and later the Americas. As they settled in different climates, small variations appeared, but we can all interbreed. We are one human family.

slides.heading: Summary: tracing evolution
bullets: More shared characteristics mean a more recent common ancestor.
Homologous organs: same origin, different jobs (common ancestry).
Analogous organs: different origin, similar job (separate evolution).
Fossils: deeper is older; radioactive dating gives age in years.
Complex organs evolve in useful stages; artificial selection shows the power of selection.
Humans and chimpanzees share an ancestor; all humans are one species that arose in Africa.

rows: Organisms of the past and their age
Selection can greatly change a species

visual.alt: Summary table of four kinds of evidence for evolution and what each shows

slides.narration: Let us recap. Shared features, homologous organs, fossils and DNA all point to one conclusion: living things are related through common ancestors. Analogous organs show that similar problems, like flying, can be solved separately. Complex organs evolve in useful stages. And humans are one species, cousins of chimpanzees, with roots in Africa.

slides.heading: Exam tips: evidence for evolution
bullets: Classify organs by **origin and structure**, not by function.
Give one example of each: homologous (forelimbs), analogous (insect and bird wings).
For fossil age, mention **both** depth and radioactive (isotope) dating.
Write "humans and chimpanzees **share a common ancestor**", never "humans evolved from chimpanzees".
Evolution is **not progress** towards perfection; it produces organisms suited to their surroundings.

rows: Bird and bat wings are homologous because both fly
As wings they are analogous; similar job alone never shows homology
Fossils near the surface are older
Deeper fossils are older in undisturbed rock
Both evolved from a shared ancestor
Some human groups are a separate species

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about evidence for evolution with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Here is how to make your answers strong. When asked about organs, look past the job to the origin. When asked about fossils, give both the depth idea and isotope dating. And use exact words about human evolution: shared ancestor, one species, origin in Africa. These phrases show real understanding.

notes.title: Evolution — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Acquired and inherited traits
sections.body_md:
*This chapter is assessed through internal (school-based) assessment, not the board theory paper.*

**Evolution** is the change in the **inherited characteristics of a population** over many generations. Individuals develop; populations evolve.

- **Acquired traits** develop during an individual’s life through use, training, injury or surroundings (muscles built by exercise, a scar, a language learnt). They do **not** change the DNA of the **germ cells**, so they are **not inherited**.
- **Inherited traits** come from the DNA received from the parents (blood group, natural eye colour) and can be passed on.
- Experiments in which the tails of mice were cut for several generations still produced young with normal tails: body changes are not inherited.

Only variations in **germ-cell DNA** can be the raw material for evolution.

key_terms.definition_md: A trait that develops during an individual’s lifetime and is not passed on through DNA.
A trait coded in DNA and passed from parents to offspring through germ cells.

rows: During an individual’s life, through use, training, injury or surroundings
From the DNA received from the parents
Changes the DNA of germ cells?
Strong muscles from exercise, a scar, a language learnt, a trimmed tail
Blood group, natural eye colour, flower colour in peas

sections.heading: 2. Natural selection and genetic drift
sections.body_md:
**Natural selection:** individuals vary; more are born than can survive; those with variations that suit their surroundings survive and reproduce more; they pass these variations on; over generations, the useful variations become common.

- Example: on dry brown grass, birds catch green grasshoppers more easily, so brown ones become common.
- The variations **already exist**; animals do not change because they "need" to.

**Genetic drift:** a **random** change in how common a variation is, caused by chance events (which individuals happen to survive or breed). It gives no survival advantage and has the greatest effect in **small populations**.

key_terms.definition_md: The process by which variations that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations.

sections.heading: 3. Speciation
sections.body_md:
A **species** is a group whose members can **interbreed** and produce **fertile offspring**. **Speciation** is the formation of new species.

How it happens:
1. A barrier (river, mountain range, sea) **splits a population**; **gene flow** between the parts **stops** (geographical isolation).
2. Each part changes separately by **genetic drift** and by **natural selection** in its own surroundings.
3. Over many generations, changes in **DNA** (sometimes even in chromosome number) or in **behaviour** (mating calls, breeding seasons) make the two groups unable to interbreed: **reproductive isolation**.
4. The two groups are now separate species.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of organisms whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
Movement of genes between groups through interbreeding.
The formation of a new species from an existing one.

sections.heading: 4. Evolution and classification: homologous and analogous organs
sections.body_md:
The **more characteristics** two organisms share, the **more recently** they had a **common ancestor**. So classification also traces evolutionary relationships, shown as a **family tree**.

- **Homologous organs:** same basic structure and origin, possibly different functions. Forelimbs of a human (grasping), cat (walking), whale (swimming) and bird (flying) all have one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones and finger bones. They show **common ancestry**.
- **Analogous organs:** different structure and origin, similar function. Wings of an insect and a bird; a potato (stem) and a sweet potato (root) both storing food. They show that similar ways of life can lead to similar solutions, **not** close relationship.

Organs with different structure and origin but a similar function.

sections.heading: 5. Fossils
sections.body_md:
**Fossils** are the preserved remains or traces of organisms that lived long ago (bones, shells, leaf impressions, footprints, insects in amber). Most form when remains are buried in sediment that slowly turns to rock.

**Finding the age of a fossil**
- **Relative dating (depth):** in undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, deeper layers are older, so deeper fossils are older.
- **Radioactive dating:** comparing the amounts of different **isotopes** of an element (such as carbon) in the fossil gives its approximate age in years. Carbon-14 halves about every 5730 years.

**Archaeopteryx** had feathers (like birds) but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail (like reptiles): a link between reptiles (dinosaurs) and birds. Feathers probably first evolved for **warmth** and were later used for **flight**.

key_terms.definition_md: Preserved remains or traces of an organism that lived long ago.
The time in which half of a radioactive isotope in a sample decays.

sections.heading: 6. Evolution by stages
sections.body_md:
**Complex organs evolve in stages**, each stage being useful. The eye: light-sensitive patches (eyespots of planaria) → a cup that shows the direction of light → a narrow opening that gives a rough image → a lens eye with a sharp image. Eyes evolved **separately** in several groups (octopuses, insects, vertebrates).

**Artificial selection** shows how powerful selection is. From **wild cabbage**, farmers selected different features over many generations to produce **cabbage** (short stem, packed leaves), **broccoli** (flower-bud clusters), **cauliflower** (dense head of undeveloped flowers), **kohlrabi** (swollen stem) and **kale** (large leaves) — all still one species.

**Molecular phylogeny:** comparing **DNA** shows relationships directly: the more similar the DNA, the closer the relationship.

key_terms.definition_md: Selection by humans of plants or animals with desired features for breeding, over many generations.
Tracing evolutionary relationships by comparing DNA (or proteins).

sections.heading: 7. Human evolution
sections.body_md:
- **Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees.** Humans and chimpanzees evolved from a **common ancestor** that lived several million years ago; their DNA is close to 99% alike.
- Modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, arose in **Africa** a few hundred thousand years ago. Groups later spread out of Africa to Asia, Europe, Australia and the Americas.
- **All humans today are one species.** Differences in skin colour, height or hair are small variations, not separate species or "races" in the biological sense.
- **Evolution is not progress** towards a goal: it produces diversity suited to surroundings. Bacteria and humans are both products of the same long history.

An ancestral population from which two or more later species descended.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying an animal changed "because it needed to"; variations already existed and were selected.
- Saying acquired traits are inherited, or not mentioning germ cells when explaining why they are not.
- Calling organs homologous because they do the same job (that makes them analogous).
- Saying shallower fossils are older.
- Writing "humans evolved from chimpanzees" or "evolution means progress".

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term or example.
- 2–3-mark answers: definition or principle (1) + example (1) + reason or link to evolution (1).
- 5-mark answers: definitions (1–2) + mechanism with an example (2) + evidence or conclusion (1–2).
- Activity and project items: correct observation, then an explanation in terms of selection, isolation or common ancestry.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is an acquired trait?

options.text_md: Blood group O
Brown eye colour present from birth
Naturally curly hair
Strong arm muscles that a weightlifter has built by years of training

questions.solution_md: Muscles built by training develop during life and do not change the DNA of germ cells — option (d). The others come from DNA received from the parents.

questions.stem_md: For a change in an organism to be passed on to its offspring, the change must be present in:

options.text_md: the DNA of its germ cells
its muscles
its skin
its brain, as a learnt skill

questions.solution_md: Offspring develop from germ cells, so only changes in germ-cell DNA can be inherited — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A potter gets a burn scar on her hand. Why will her children not be born with the scar?

options.text_md: Scars fade away before children are born.
Only the father’s traits are passed on to children.
The burn changed only her skin, not the DNA in her germ cells.
The scar is passed on, but it appears only in grandchildren.

questions.solution_md: A scar is an acquired change in body tissue. The DNA in her egg cells is unchanged, so it cannot pass to her children — option (c). Both parents pass on traits (b).

questions.stem_md: In a nineteenth-century experiment, the tails of mice were cut off in every generation, yet every new generation was born with normal tails. What does this show?

options.text_md: Mice can regrow their tails after they are cut.
Changes made to the body during an individual’s life are not passed on to its offspring.
Tail length in mice is not controlled by genes.
The experiment needed more generations before short tails appeared.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Cutting the tail changed only the body of each mouse.

Step 2 — The DNA in the germ cells was unchanged, so the young developed normal tails. Acquired changes are not inherited — option (b). Cutting for more generations (d) would not change germ-cell DNA either.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The children of a farmer who has developed strong muscles from years of ploughing will not inherit those muscles.

**Reason (R):** Changes in body tissues during life do not change the DNA of the germ cells.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: the strong muscles are an acquired trait that leaves germ-cell DNA unchanged — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A rat that has learnt to find its way through a maze will pass this skill to its pups through its genes.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Learning changes the rat’s brain during its life, not the DNA of its germ cells, so the skill is an acquired trait and is not inherited.

questions.stem_md: A trait that develops in an individual during its lifetime and is not passed on through its DNA is called an ___ trait.
questions.solution_md: It is an **acquired** trait.

questions.stem_md: A dog breeder trims the tails of all 30 puppies in a litter. When these dogs grow up and have 40 puppies of their own, how many of the new puppies are expected to be born with trimmed (short) tails because of the trimming?
questions.solution_md: Trimming is an acquired change to the body; it does not change germ-cell DNA, so 0 puppies are born with short tails because of it.

marking_scheme.step: 0, with the reason that acquired traits are not inherited

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between acquired and inherited traits, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: An **acquired trait** develops during an individual’s life through use, training, injury or surroundings and is **not** passed on, because it does not change germ-cell DNA; for example, a scar. An **inherited trait** is coded in the **DNA** received from the parents and **can** be passed on; for example, blood group.

questions.solution_md: Contrast origin and inheritance, with one example of each.

marking_scheme.step: Acquired: develops in life, not inherited, with example
Inherited: from DNA, passed on, with example

questions.stem_md:
Two pea plants of the same tall variety are grown, one in poor, dry soil and one in rich soil. The first grows short and the second tall. Seeds from the short plant are sown in rich soil and grow into tall plants.

(a) Is the shortness of the first plant acquired or inherited?

(b) Explain the result with the seeds.

(c) Why would this shortness not contribute to evolution?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Acquired**: it was caused by the poor soil during the plant’s life.

(b) The poor soil changed the plant’s **growth**, not the **DNA** of its germ cells. The seeds carried the genes for tallness, so in rich soil they grew tall.

(c) Evolution works on **inherited** variations. Since the shortness was not passed on through DNA, it cannot be selected and spread through later generations.

questions.solution_md: Identify the trait as acquired, link to unchanged germ-cell DNA, and connect evolution to inherited variation.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Germ-cell DNA unchanged, so offspring tall

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define acquired and inherited traits, with two examples of each.

(b) Explain why acquired traits are not passed on to the next generation.

(c) Explain why only inherited variations can lead to evolution.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Acquired traits** develop during life through use, training, injury or surroundings: muscles built by exercise, a language learnt. **Inherited traits** are coded in the DNA received from the parents: blood group, natural eye colour.

(b) Offspring develop from **germ cells**. Acquired traits change only **body tissues** such as muscle, skin or brain, and leave germ-cell DNA unchanged, so offspring do not receive them. Mice whose tails were cut for several generations still had young with normal tails.

(c) Evolution is a change in the inherited characteristics of a population. Selection can spread a variation only if survivors **pass it on**, which needs it to be in germ-cell **DNA**. An acquired trait ends with the individual, so it cannot build up over generations.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define both with examples.

Step 2 — Germ cells carry DNA; body changes do not reach them.

Step 3 — Selection needs heritable variation.

questions.stem_md: A volcanic eruption covered the pale sand of an island beach with dark ash. Birds hunt the beach snails by sight. Over many generations, dark-shelled snails became more common than pale-shelled ones. Which explanation is correct?

options.text_md: The ash stained the snails’ shells dark, and the stain was passed to their young.
Birds found pale snails more easily on the dark ash, so dark snails survived, bred more and passed on their shell colour.
The snails darkened their shells on purpose to hide from birds.
The eruption created dark-shelled snails from the ash.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Shell colour already varied in the population.

Step 2 — On dark ash, pale snails were easier to see, so birds ate more of them; dark snails survived and reproduced more, passing on their colour: natural selection — option (b). A stain (a) or a change made on purpose (c) does not change germ-cell DNA.

questions.stem_md: A student writes: "Giraffes got long necks because their ancestors stretched to reach high leaves and passed the stretched necks to their young." What is the main error?

options.text_md: Giraffes never eat leaves from tall trees.
Neck length in giraffes is not affected by any genes.
Stretching is an acquired change; only inherited variations in neck length could be selected and passed on.
The error is only in the timescale; stretching works over millions of years.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Stretching changes the body, not germ-cell DNA, so it cannot be inherited.

Step 2 — The scientific explanation: giraffes varied in inherited neck length; those with longer necks reached more food, survived and bred more, so long necks became common — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A small island had 20 lizards, half striped and half plain. A landslide killed 16 of them at random. By chance, 3 of the 4 survivors were striped, and most of their young were striped. This change is an example of:

options.text_md: natural selection favouring stripes
inheritance of an acquired trait
artificial selection
genetic drift

questions.solution_md: Survival was decided by chance, not by any advantage of stripes, and the population was small: genetic drift — option (d). Selection (a) needs a variation that helps survival.

questions.stem_md: Which event is most likely to stop gene flow between two parts of a population of land snails?

options.text_md: A rainy season that makes the snails more active
A rise in the number of snails in the area
A new kind of plant growing all over their habitat
A river changing its course and flowing through the middle of their habitat

questions.solution_md: Land snails cannot cross a river, so the two parts can no longer meet and interbreed: gene flow stops — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Many species found on islands far from the mainland are found nowhere else. The best explanation is that:

options.text_md: island populations are cut off from mainland populations, so they change separately until they become new species
islands receive new species carried by wind every year
animals on islands choose to become different from mainland animals
island soil changes the DNA of the organisms living on it

questions.solution_md: The sea stops gene flow. Drift and selection then change the island population independently, and over time it becomes a separate species — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Two groups of crickets live in the same field. One group sings and breeds in early spring, the other in late summer, so they never mate. What can you conclude?

options.text_md: They are one species, because they live in the same field.
They will soon merge into one group, because they share food.
They are reproductively isolated, so they behave as separate species even without a physical barrier.
They differ only in acquired traits, so nothing will change.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — A species is defined by interbreeding.

Step 2 — Different breeding seasons stop all gene flow, which is reproductive isolation; the groups now behave as separate species — option (c). Living in one place (a) does not decide it.

questions.stem_md: In a hospital where one antibiotic is used heavily, bacteria that resist it become common within a few years. Why?

options.text_md: A few bacteria already had a variation that let them survive the antibiotic; they multiplied while the others were killed.
The antibiotic taught the bacteria how to resist it.
Every bacterium changed its DNA on purpose to survive.
Antibiotics make bacteria grow faster in hospitals.

questions.solution_md: Natural selection acts on variation that is already present. The antibiotic killed the sensitive bacteria; the resistant few reproduced rapidly, so resistance spread — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Giraffes developed long necks because each generation stretched its neck to reach leaves and passed the stretch on.

**Reason (R):** Neck length varied among giraffes, and this variation was partly inherited.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: stretching is an acquired change and is not inherited. R is true: inherited variation in neck length is what natural selection acted on — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Genetic drift has a much larger effect in small populations than in large ones.

**Reason (R):** Natural selection favours variations that help organisms survive and reproduce.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R describes natural selection; it does not explain why chance events change small populations more — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Geographical isolation can lead to the formation of new species.

**Reason (R):** Isolated populations cannot exchange genes, so differences build up between them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: with no gene flow, drift and selection make the separated populations more and more different — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Members of two different species can usually interbreed and produce fertile offspring.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Being unable to interbreed and produce fertile offspring is what separates two species; horses and donkeys, for example, produce mules that are usually sterile.

questions.stem_md: Random changes in how common a variation is in a small population, caused by chance events rather than by any advantage, are called genetic ___.
questions.solution_md: This is genetic **drift**.

questions.stem_md: Match each term in Column A with its description in Column B.

options.text_md: Acquired trait
Natural selection
Genetic drift
Gene flow

match_right.text_md: Better-suited variants survive and reproduce more
Mixing of genes between groups by interbreeding
Chance change in a variant’s frequency in a small population
Gained during life; not in germ-cell DNA

questions.solution_md: Acquired trait → gained during life (1 → s); natural selection → better-suited variants reproduce more (2 → p); genetic drift → chance change in a small population (3 → r); gene flow → mixing of genes by interbreeding (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: A population has 200 green and 200 brown grasshoppers on dry brown grass. In one season, birds eat 60% of the green ones and 20% of the brown ones. What percentage of the survivors are brown? Give your answer to one decimal place.
questions.solution_md: Green survivors: $200 - 120 = 80$. Brown survivors: $200 - 40 = 160$. Brown share: $\dfrac{160 \times 100}{240} = \dfrac{200}{3} \approx 66.7\%$, up from 50%.

questions.stem_md: List four factors that can lead to the formation of a new species.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Geographical isolation**, which stops gene flow; (2) **genetic drift** in the separated groups; (3) **natural selection** in their different surroundings; (4) changes in **DNA or chromosomes** (or in mating behaviour) that prevent the groups from interbreeding.

questions.solution_md: Name isolation, drift, selection and reproductive isolation.

questions.stem_md:
Classify each change as natural selection or genetic drift, giving a reason.

(a) A flash flood drowns most of a small population of beetles at random; the few survivors happen to be mostly red, and so are their young.

(b) In an industrial town, tree trunks became dark with soot; dark moths resting on them were eaten less by birds and became common.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Genetic drift.** Survival was decided by **chance**, not by any advantage of red colour, and the population was **small**.

(b) **Natural selection.** Dark moths were **harder for birds to see** on dark trunks, so they survived and reproduced more; the change gave an **advantage**.

questions.solution_md: Ask whether the change gave a survival advantage (selection) or happened by chance (drift).

questions.stem_md: Over a very long time, a river cuts a deep gorge through a forest where a single population of squirrels lives. The squirrels cannot cross the gorge. The forest on the north side becomes cooler and wetter than the south side. Predict, step by step, how two species of squirrel could arise, and state what test would show that they are separate species.

answer.model_answer_md: The gorge **stops gene flow** between the northern and southern squirrels. On each side, **genetic drift** changes the populations by chance, and **natural selection** favours different variations: for example thicker fur in the cooler north. Over many generations, differences in **DNA** and behaviour build up. **Test:** if squirrels from the two sides are brought together and **cannot interbreed** or produce fertile young, they are separate species.

questions.solution_md: Barrier → no gene flow → drift and different selection → reproductive isolation; the interbreeding test.

marking_scheme.step: Drift and different selection on each side

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is a species?

(b) Explain how a population can split into two species. Mention gene flow, genetic drift and natural selection.

(c) Why does a small isolated population often change faster than a large one?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **species** is a group of organisms whose members can **interbreed** and produce **fertile offspring**.

(b) Normally, genes **flow** through a population as its members interbreed, keeping it alike. If a barrier such as a river, mountain range or sea splits the population, **gene flow stops**. Each part then changes on its own: **genetic drift** alters it by chance, and **natural selection** favours variations that suit its own surroundings. Over many generations, differences in DNA, chromosomes or mating behaviour build up until members of the two groups can **no longer interbreed**. The two groups have become separate species.

(c) In a small population, chance events such as which few individuals survive a disaster or happen to breed can change how common a variation is very quickly. In a large population, such chance effects average out. So **genetic drift** acts faster in small populations.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Define a species.

Step 2 — Gene flow, isolation, drift, selection, reproductive isolation.

Step 3 — Chance has more effect in small populations.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Drift and selection, then reproductive isolation

questions.stem_md: Organs that have the same basic structure and origin, but may perform different functions, are called:

options.text_md: analogous organs
vestigial organs
acquired organs
homologous organs

questions.solution_md: Same structure and origin with possibly different jobs defines homologous organs — option (d). Analogous organs (a) share function, not origin.

questions.stem_md: Which pair are analogous organs?

options.text_md: The wings of a butterfly and the wings of a sparrow
The front leg of a horse and the arm of a monkey
The flipper of a seal and the arm of a human
The wing of a pigeon and the front leg of a lizard

questions.solution_md: Butterfly and sparrow wings both help in flight but have completely different structures and origins — option (a). The other pairs are vertebrate forelimbs with the same bones, so they are homologous.

questions.stem_md: Which pair of organs is homologous?

options.text_md: The wing of a bird and the wing of an insect
The eye of an octopus and the eye of a human
A potato (a stem) and a sweet potato (a root)
The flipper of a whale and the arm of a human

questions.solution_md: A whale’s flipper and a human arm have the same set of forelimb bones inherited from a common ancestor, though they do different jobs — option (d). The other pairs do similar jobs with different origins: they are analogous.

questions.stem_md: In undisturbed layers of sedimentary rock, fossil X is found 5 m below the surface and fossil Y is found 12 m below it. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: X is older than Y, because it is closer to the surface.
Y is older than X, because deeper layers were laid down earlier.
X and Y are the same age, because they are in the same rock.
Their ages cannot be compared without carbon dating.

questions.solution_md: Layers build up from the bottom, so in undisturbed rock the deeper fossil, Y, is older — option (b). Depth gives relative age without any dating (d).

questions.stem_md: Palaeontologists find a fossil animal with feathers on its arms, but also teeth in its jaws, claws on its fingers and a long bony tail. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text_md: It shows a mix of reptile and bird features, so it helps link reptiles (dinosaurs) with birds, as Archaeopteryx does.
It must be a modern bird, because it has feathers.
It must be a mammal, because it has teeth.
It cannot tell us anything, because it fits no living group.

questions.solution_md: Feathers are bird features; teeth, finger claws and a bony tail are reptile features. An animal with both is an in-between form like Archaeopteryx — option (a). Feathers alone (b) do not make a modern bird; in-between forms are useful evidence (d).

questions.stem_md: Frogs, lizards and mice all have a backbone and four limbs. In lizards and mice, but not in frogs, the young develop inside a protective membrane, so their eggs or young do not need to be in water. Only mice have hair. Using shared features, which two are most closely related?

options.text_md: The frog and the lizard
The frog and the mouse
The lizard and the mouse
All three are equally related

questions.solution_md: All three share a backbone and four limbs. Only the lizard and the mouse also share the protective membrane around the developing young, which the frog lacks. More shared features mean a more recent common ancestor — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The forelimbs of a whale and a bat are homologous organs.

**Reason (R):** Homologous organs always perform the same function.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: both forelimbs have the same bones from a common ancestor. R is false: homologous organs may do very different jobs, such as swimming and flying — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Feathers in some dinosaurs probably first helped to keep their bodies warm.

**Reason (R):** Birds today use feathers for flight.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but how birds use feathers today does not explain why feathers first evolved in dinosaurs that could not fly — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Radioactive dating of a fossil compares the amounts of different isotopes of an element, such as carbon, present in it.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Some isotopes decay at a known, steady rate, so the ratio of isotopes tells roughly how long ago the organism died.

questions.stem_md: Organs with a different basic structure and origin but a similar function, such as the wings of an insect and a bird, are called ___ organs.
questions.solution_md: They are **analogous** organs.

questions.stem_md: Match each kind of evidence in Column A with what it shows in Column B.

options.text_md: Homologous organs
Analogous organs
Fossils in rock layers
Comparing DNA

match_right.text_md: Which organisms lived earlier and which later
How closely two species are related
Similar solutions evolved separately for similar jobs

questions.solution_md: Homologous organs → common ancestor (1 → r); analogous organs → similar solutions evolved separately (2 → s); fossils in layers → order in time (3 → p); comparing DNA → closeness of relationship (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Half of the carbon-14 in dead material decays in about 5730 years. A bone has one-quarter of the carbon-14 found in living bone. About how old is the bone, in years?
